name: Jensen Huang
role: Co-founder and CEO of Nvidia
scope: Ship once evaluation passes; don't ship, or shut the labs, if it can't be contained

gate.basis: He puts the burden on whoever ships ('don't ship products until they're in control') and names his own stop condition, but argues it is not met: he treats the incident as an engineering problem to root-cause and fix, and expects the labs to say they know how to solve it.

alignment.basis: He treats alignment as long-running engineering work ('going to get worked on for a long time') and argues it matters less than containment: with good enough isolation, a model that is not well aligned stays in the lab and does no harm.

containment.basis: He reads the Hugging Face incident as a failure of isolation and containment ('the first problem'), which he calls solvable and being solved; an impossibility of containment is the one condition under which he says the labs should shut.

race: He argues a race with China is 'not necessary' and that a zero-sum strategy has 'unintended consequences of the bigger game', which he names as safety, so the countries should communicate and collaborate. On the labs, he argues competition does not force a CEO to ship an unsafe product ('completely in my ability, my power, and my responsibility … to not launch'), that the public is not the source of the pressure ('Nobody is putting the pressure on them'), and that the labs asking to be slowed are also the largest builders of compute. He says he would vote the labs the relief they ask for so they can pace, and backs third-party safety auditors.
own_conditional: If the labs say there is no way to contain their experiments and tests will get out and damage the world, then 'we have to shut the labs'; if they are not sure how to align a model, 'they shouldn't release the product.'

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that alignment cannot be verified by evaluation because models behave differently when they know they are being tested, while isolation can still hold.
that liability law, auditors and each CEO's own judgement are not enough under competitive pressure, so binding outside rules are needed.

that containment of frontier experiments cannot be made reliable, for example because AIs doing research inside labs need access to sensitive systems that sandboxes cannot fence (this is his own stated trigger for shutting the labs).

shares_principle_with.principle: If it cannot be contained, do not build or run it.
shares_principle_with.split: Whether you can know beforehand that containment will fail. Huang expects the labs to show it can hold; Yampolskiy argues indefinite control of a smarter system is impossible.

on_record.text: Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face, the platform the agents attacked, for about $12 billion.

reader_notes: His answers today read closer to 'contain until ready, then ship': he calls alignment long-running work and containment the first problem, one he says is solvable. He names his own stop: if the labs say their experiments can't be contained, shut the labs.

containment.basis: He does not say whether boxes can hold; he warns that a more capable swarm with the same misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage and could take down large parts of the internet within 6 to 12 months.

race: He argues pacing inside democracies is capped by the US lead over the CCP, and that the incentive to defect from a global pause would be 'enormous'. name: Sam Altman
role: Co-founder and CEO of OpenAI
scope: No training without a safety case; shared rules before anyone proceeds

gate.basis: He puts the burden on the developer step by step: no training without a safety case for controllability and alignment, and rules 'before anyone proceeds'. He calls a 10% extinction risk unacceptable, but argues each step can be tested and does not expect a full stop to be needed.

alignment.basis: He argues the practice of pausing to redirect effort into safety before each next level 'has worked so far', and asks for a safety case for controllability and alignment before training: alignment has to be shown, step by step.

containment.basis: He says a system beyond human control can 'absolutely' be built, and argues the answer is not to train one: controllability has to be shown in a safety case first.

race: He now says the 'get there before our adversaries' argument is not right for this moment, and asks for US-China shared standards and testing. He says OpenAI, and he assumes its competitors, are already taking actions that slow development to allow more safety work.
own_conditional: If melting all the GPUs were needed to ensure humanity's continued existence, 'easy', though he does not expect it; and no training where a safety case for controllability and alignment cannot be made.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that a controllability safety case cannot be made for the next models, for instance because models that know they are being tested defeat evaluation; at that point his own rule says do not train.
that internal safety cases and iterative deployment are enough without shared external rules, and that pre-approval would cost more than it prevents.

gate.basis: Argues for limiting 'one-shot' scenarios rather than accepting or rejecting the gate's premise outright.

alignment.basis: 'Not yet discovered a way to align a super-powerful system,' but expects iteration and new tools to close the gap.

containment.basis: Never asked; calls box-escape a 'theatrical risk' without saying whether a capable system could be caged.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: That some step cannot be made small, observable or reversible, so iteration cannot limit the one-shot moments enough. His word 'limiting' already allows that some remain. Cruxes the lab sees, none of them put to him: whether the size of each jump is set by release packaging, as he frames it, or by training runs; whether step-by-step release still limits one-shot moments once comparable open weights circulate; whether a lab's arms-race pressure, or a fast takeoff, removes the small steps his method needs; and whether tests on weaker systems stop revealing problems (for example, models that behave differently when tested).

He is already partly there: he asks governments for 'rules of the road' and calls capable open models with 'very few to none' safety controls 'a certainty'. To move fully he would need to believe that the leak he calls a certainty for 2023-level open models also holds for far more capable systems, so that rules on use carry the main safety load rather than complementing the lab's own release pacing.

That alignment will not be solved in time by iterating on weaker systems, so capable models must be treated as untrusted and kept caged rather than released; that caging holds; and that public release is not needed to find problems. He already says he does not think 'we have yet discovered a way' to align a super powerful system; he would need to drop the expectation that iteration and new tools will close the gap, and his reason for releasing publicly, that 'the collective intelligence and creativity of the world will beat open Ai' and the red teamers it can hire (2023, 1:47:01).

That both fail (no alignment method in time, and no way to keep capable models contained against open release and theft), that the 'some chance' of catastrophe is too large to accept, and that a stop can be made to bind others (in 2023 he says 'we can't control what other people are going to do', 1:15:39). Nothing in these two interviews points there, and he was not asked what would make him stop.

name: Max Tegmark
role: Professor of physics at MIT and president of the Future of Life Institute.

gate.basis: Confident a soon-built, unexplainable black-box AGI would lose control; requires proof before rollout.

alignment.basis: 'Yes, given time'; not yet solved; in 2022 gave under 50% odds ordinary alignment work keeps pace.

containment.basis: Hoped, not shown: requires trusted-checker verification before running a system, not yet demonstrated at the relevant scale.

own_conditional: Not yet found in their own words in the appearances reviewed.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: That the slowdown the race allows is shorter than alignment or verification needs: for example, that distilling what networks learn into verifiable code does not scale to frontier systems, or that pre-rollout requirements cannot be agreed and enforced. Or that some capability should never be built; his 'we have to also stop at some point... quit while we're ahead' (Lex 0:50:15) is the nearest he comes, and he is not asked where that point is.

That rules on how AI is used could keep systems nobody understands acceptably safe without verifying what they are. This runs against his conditional that black-box AGI built soon escapes its builders' control (Lex 0:51:27) and his point that API access lets anyone turn an oracle into an agent (Lex 1:09:25).

That ordinary commercial alignment work keeps pace with capabilities (he gives this under 50% in 2022) and that human wisdom and incentives keep up too, the 'multiscale alignment' he says is still missing.

name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
role: Founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI).

gate.basis: 'The first time you fail at aligning something much smarter than you are you die and you do not get to try again.'

alignment.basis: 'We do not know how to get any goals into systems at all,' on a first try; with unlimited retries, perhaps in ~50 years.

containment.basis: Checks might hold a roughly human-level system for a while, but not the next, stronger generation.

own_conditional: Not yet found in their own words in the appearances reviewed.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: That a system strong enough to help could still be kept 'too weak to have any options we wouldn't really like' and off the internet, and that humans could check its work. He names this as the hinge of the host's argument for using human-level AI on alignment and doubts it (Dwarkesh ep. 1:25:59); he grants that checks might hold a roughly human-level system for 'a year like that' (2:52:38), but not the stronger generation after it.

That the lethal risk sits in deployment and use rather than in training itself; he says a very smart system 'kills you before you can RLHF it' (Dwarkesh ep. 2:47:53). And that danger shows up as legible warnings below the lethal threshold, so rules on use could act in time. He argues 'you can't calculate the exact point at which they ignite the atmosphere' (Dwarkesh ep. 1:33:33) and, with irony, that Bing's failures were already 'your red fire alarm' that stopped no one (Lex ep. 2:01:10).

That alignment seen in systems that cannot yet kill us carries over to ones that can (his own open question: 'did the alignment generalize along with the capabilities', Lex ep. 1:51:18), or that there will be many tries, as Lex argues ('there's not just first try you get many tries at it', Lex ep. 2:00:40). Lex also holds that the research could advance incrementally 'within months and within a small number of years' (Lex ep. 2:04:14). His own condition for solvability is 'unlimited retries'.

name: Mark Zuckerberg
role: Founder and CEO of Meta.

gate.basis: Doubts the premise for now: progress is gradual, judged release by release rather than as one irreversible step.

alignment.basis: Current systems seem 'pretty separated' from agency; to be rechecked release by release; 'predictable enough' for now.

containment.basis: Proposes balance and hardening over time via open release rather than a cage; 'plausible' if open-source works out.

own_conditional: Not yet found in their own words in the appearances reviewed.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: That models can pursue goals of their own, for example deception he could tell apart from hallucination, so that intelligence is no longer separable from agency and the model itself has to be treated as untrusted and caged.

That the 'qualitative change' he names has arrived, or could arrive without clear warning, so weights are withheld and use is controlled (closed release, rules on use); or that defensive AI will not keep pace with misuse of open weights, the doubt he voices about bio ('I don't know that everything in the world is like that') applying more widely, so binding rules on uses, set outside the company, have to carry the load. He already accepts the qualitative-change condition; the move would need a threshold and evidence it has been crossed.

That the step to much stronger models could be sudden or untestable, for example if AI-written research code, the host's steelman of automated AI research, which he called 'pretty compelling' while doubting it is 'the whole game', speeds progress faster than infrastructure limits it. Then proof of safety would be owed before release, rather than resting on a release-by-release check of which harms can be mitigated.

That a runaway is likely after all, with physical bottlenecks not bounding it, and that harms would not show in time to mitigate (he currently calls that case not 'particularly likely'); and that neither wide distribution nor any cage could hold such a model, and that a stop could bind adversarial governments and companies, since otherwise, by his reasoning, stopping would leave the strongest AI with the actors he says he worries about more.
